summary: Addresses how to protect the integrity of data in a routing policy system. It provides an authentication and authorization model so that only the right parties can change routing policy information. It is a standards-track document at the proposed standard level.

plainLanguage.summary: If anyone could edit the road map, drivers would get lost. This makes sure only the right people can change it.

questions: how is routing policy data secured
subtitle: Who may add, change or delete entries in a routing registry, and how the registry proves it.

tldr.problem: Routing registries such as the IRR were first used only to document routing policy for debugging, with very weak authentication. As they came to be used to configure the Internet, adding bad data became a real threat to routing integrity.
tldr.mechanism: Maintainer objects hold authentication methods, and a hierarchical authorization model ties additions of route, address and AS number data to the objects that cover them, with new attributes such as mnt-routes, mnt-lower and reclaim.
tldr.outcome: The RFC defines authentication and authorization for changes to registry data, but not for queries, and it does not define a fully distributed registry. It was later updated by RFC 4012.

facts.label: RIPE schema size
facts.value: about 80 attribute types, about 15 object types

today: RFC 2725 is a Proposed Standard that has been updated by RFC 4012; it has not been obsoleted. Check the updating RFC for later changes.

sections.title: Why Registries Need Security
sections.content:
The Internet Routing Registry (IRR) is a set of repositories for routing policy information. Its early role was advisory: documenting intended routing policy for debugging, where a very weak form of authentication was judged sufficient. It is increasingly used for purposes that need stronger integrity, and this document aims to keep data trustworthy even if the IRR is spread over less trusted repositories.

The RFC traces the history. The NSFNET policy routing database (PRDB) decided who could announce which prefixes to the NSFNET backbone, using manual confirmation, but served a single organization. The RIPE database formats were the basis of the original IRR, and the Routing Policy System Language (RPSL) added support for CIDR and aggregation. Four needs are listed: many organizations' policies, CIDR complexity, integrity with delegated authority, and integrity with distributed storage. This document addresses the third, and says a separate document will be needed for the fourth.

The reasoning is that routing protocols give no assurance that a route origination is legitimate, and CIDR lets a more specific prefix override a less specific one. Without a way to know who may announce a prefix, there is an opening for an effective denial of service attack. The existing system sends notifications on changes but gives inadequate protection against additions.
sections.plainLanguage: The phone book used to be kept for fun, so anyone could scribble in it. Now people use it to decide where mail goes, so scribbles could send mail to the wrong place.

sections.title: Assumptions and Scope
sections.content:
The authorization model assumes a few policies. Address space is allocated hierarchically: IANA delegates to the regional registries (named as ARIN, APNIC and RIPE), which delegate to members, who assign to customers. AS numbers are allocated singly or in small blocks, with registries holding blocks. Routes should only be announced with the consent of both the origin AS holder and the address space holder. Address and AS registries may be different entities from routing registries. Parts of the space can loosen these rules with a weak method or the authentication method none, though the notify attribute still informs involved parties.

Only authentication and authorization of additions, deletions and changes are in scope. Authentication and authorization of queries, and mutual authentication of queries, are explicitly out of scope. So is the definition of attributes for a distributed registry, and the encapsulation of transactions and exchanges between registries. The document assumes familiarity with RIPE-181 and RPSL.
sections.plainLanguage: The rules assume land is handed out from the top down: big owners give pieces to smaller ones. The RFC only worries about who may write in the book, not about who may read it.

sections.title: Goals and Requirements
sections.content:
The RFC lists problems to address: keeping the effect of accidental misconfiguration local to the provider that made it, stopping a customer from using malicious misconfiguration as a denial of service attack when providers route filter customers, and eliminating unauthorized use of address space. It notes that mistyped static routes happen regularly, and that CIDR's preference for more specific routes makes errors worse: a more specific route advertised from afar is preferred if accepted at all.

Controlling who changes data separates authentication (who is trying to make the change) from authorization (whether that identity may perform the operation). Centralized control would raise scaling problems, so authority should be delegated much like address and AS number allocation. Different parts of the database need different authentication strengths, so multiple methods must be supported per object, and weak methods must not compromise the whole database.

A route object's key has both a prefix and an origin AS, so adding one must be validated against the authorization for both. The model must handle common cases such as hierarchical allocation, aggregation with multihomed more specifics, provider independent addresses with multiple origin ASes, changing providers and renumbering grace periods. It cannot mandate one address allocation policy, and whether address space can be recovered must be selectable per object.
sections.plainLanguage: The goal is that one mistake in one place cannot mess up the whole map. Each piece of the book must be edited only by the person who owns that piece.

sections.title: Authentication Methods
sections.content:
A maintainer object holds authentication filters. Each of its auth attributes starts with a method keyword followed by the information needed to enforce it. Other objects name a maintainer in their mnt-by attribute, which grants that maintainer authority over them.

The methods listed are mail-from, a regular expression matched against the mail From or Reply-To headers, which is very weak and discouraged because mail forgery is easy; crypt-pw, a UNIX crypt password sent in clear text in the transaction, so it can be snooped and guessed; pgp-from, Merit's PGP extension, which is deprecated; and pgpkey, written PGPKEY-hhhhhhhh with the four byte PGP key id in hex, where the certificate is stored in a separate object. A further method none disables authentication, and auth may now appear in person or role objects.

Repositories may refuse weaker methods, and are encouraged to refuse the deprecated pgp-from. Any digital signature technique could in principle be used, and transactions should carry multiple signatures so a repository using only some techniques can verify at least one.
sections.plainLanguage: To write in the book you show a proof of who you are. A password mailed in the open is a weak proof, but a special signature only you can make is much stronger.

sections.title: Objects, Maintainers and Delegation
sections.content:
The model adds one object type, as-block, which records the delegation of a range of AS numbers (for example AS1321 - AS1335) to a repository. An aut-num object marks the existence of an AS, and an inetnum object records an address allocation. A route object records a route that may appear in the global routing table. A missing mnt-by means no control over changes, which is highly inadvisable, and the attribute is now mandatory in all objects.

New attributes carry delegation. mnt-routes lets named maintainers add route objects for that AS or for exact or more specific prefixes, but not change the object it sits in. mnt-lower does the same for more specific data and for hierarchical names. referral-by records which maintainer created a new maintainer and can never change. auth-override lets the referring maintainer take over a maintainer inactive for 60 days, unless the holder removes it after being notified.

reclaim lets the maintainer of a covering object modify or delete more specific objects, which supports address lending and cleanup when an organization vanishes. no-reclaim carves out exceptions. A reclaim may only be added if it does not strip the autonomy of existing more specific objects. Without either, the maintainer of a less specific object cannot change more specific ones.
sections.plainLanguage: Each owner gets a stamp, and big owners can hand out smaller stamps for smaller pieces. A big owner can keep a master key for emergencies, but only if the small owners agreed to it.

sections.title: Adding, Modifying and Deleting Objects
sections.content:
Adding a route object must pass two checks. The submission must satisfy the authentication of the aut-num for the origin AS, and of either a route object or, if none applies, an inetnum. If the aut-num does not exist, the addition is rejected. The registry looks for an exact match of the prefix, then for the longest less specific route; if none is found it uses an inetnum whose status must be allocated. Where mnt-routes is present, mnt-by is not considered for that object.

The root repository starts with an inetnum covering 0/0 and an as-block covering the full AS number range, and an initial maintainer whose referral-by refers to itself. Objects without natural hierarchy, like person and role objects, are unique only within their repository, with an external reference written RIPE::CO19. Hierarchical names such as AS1:AS-Bar must be authorized by the aut-num named left of the rightmost colon.

Modifying or deleting needs a match with a maintainer in the object, or a matching reclaim in a less specific object. A deletion is a special case of modification and may leave the object marked deleted.
sections.plainLanguage: To add a new line, you must have the permission of both the owner of the name and the owner of the land. If either one says no, the line does not go in.

sections.title: Deployment Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC says routing registries are not yet universally accepted. A minority of providers filter per prefix using the IRR, another minority do not support it, and the majority register prefixes but do not use strict prefix filtering. One cited reason is that filtering with incomplete or inaccurate registry data can break connectivity. Existing data is a major issue: many route objects refer to prefixes no longer announced, were registered with an origin AS taken from NSFNET border ASes, or were never withdrawn when CIDR aggregates replaced them. Much data has no maintainer, and most maintainers use only the weakest authentication.

A staged transition is proposed, from adding stronger authorization and schema changes for delegation, through query traversal by delegation and address registry cooperation, to hierarchical authorization for aut-num, inetnum and route objects, and finally purging data that is clearly unused with no valid contact. Cooperation among registries and address registries, which would send signed transactions, is required.
sections.plainLanguage: Switching to the new rules is hard because the old book is full of stale lines nobody erased. The plan is to tidy it up in steps.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The document's subject is authorization of additions, deletions and changes to routing policy repositories, with strong cryptographic authentication left to a companion document. Rules are designed so any party mirroring a repository can independently verify that transactions followed them, provided the mirror is complete and checks each change in order.

Authentication alone is an incomplete model, and prior practice specified authorization only for deletions and changes. These rules add additions and handle cases such as organizations that no longer exist. Authentication and authorization of queries remain out of scope.
sections.plainLanguage: Anyone keeping a copy of the book can check that every new line followed the rules, as long as they have seen all the changes in order.

Clear text password checked against UNIX crypt form
Signature identity pointing to an external key ring

items.label: Route maintainer
items.desc: Maintainers allowed to add route objects for this AS or for matching or more specific prefixes.

items.label: Lower maintainer
items.desc: Maintainers allowed to add more specific objects below this one.

items.label: Reclaim
items.desc: Lets this object's maintainer modify or delete more specific objects of the same type.

items.label: Referral
items.desc: Records the maintainer that created this maintainer; never changes.

items.label: Auth override
items.desc: Date after which the referring maintainer may modify an inactive maintainer.
